sections.h2: Recorder's office and what it records
sections.html:
Find the Franklin County Recorder on the 18th floor of the Franklin County Courthouse, 373 South High Street, Columbus. Call (614) 525-3930 or write to recorder@franklincountyohio.gov. The office records, preserves and retrieves real estate, personal property and other records so property interests are safeguarded and easy to find.

In this county the Auditor and the Recorder are separate offices. The Auditor handles ownership changes and the fees for the transfer, and the Recorder files the deed itself. Plan to visit or mail to both.

The deed goes to the Auditor first and reaches the Recorder afterward. The sequence runs like this:

  • Prepare a new deed form. A template is available through the County Law Library under real estate forms.
  • Copy the legal description from the last deed on file, which the Recorder's website lets you search, and follow the county document standards.
  • Sign the deed in front of a notary.
  • File the deed with the Auditor and pay the Auditor's transfer charges.
  • Include a separate payment for the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards the deed to the Recorder once the transfer is complete.

Most owners never write a deed from scratch. If a title company or attorney is handling your sale, it drafts the deed from the prior recorded one and walks it through each step. Writing it yourself works only if you are comfortable copying a legal description exactly and following the county document standards, since a document that fails them costs an extra $20.

Paying off a mortgage does not call for a new deed. The lender files a release of mortgage as its own document.

Fees follow Ohio Revised Code 317.32, and the Recorder offers a fee calculator for checking your math.

Franklin County Recorder fees
ChargeFee
First two pages$34
Each additional page$8

Each indexed marginal reference$4

Make checks and money orders payable to the Franklin County Recorder, since checks payable to second or third parties are refused. Cards are limited to Discover, Mastercard and Visa. The $34 and $8 figures each combine a base fee with a housing trust fund fee of the same amount.

The Auditor's transfer and conveyance office handles more than 30,000 property transfers a year. The conveyance fee is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, made up of $1 per $1,000 set by the State of Ohio and $2 per $1,000 set by the Board of Commissioners. There is also a $3 minimum and a $0.50 transfer tax on any transfer that is not exempt. An exempt transfer owes only the $0.50.

If the seller is receiving the homestead exemption at the time of transfer, the county's $2 piece is waived and the fee drops to $1 per $1,000. You can verify homestead status on the Auditor's property search under the Homestead Credit entry on the parcel summary. Round the sale amount up to the next $100 when you use the calculator.

  • Pay by cash, business check or cashier's check made out to the Franklin County Auditor.
  • Personal checks are not accepted, and the office can give change only on cash.
  • Do not add payments for other county offices to the same check.
  • Transfers must carry the exact amount to be processed.

Questions go to the Transfer and Conveyance Department at 614-525-3253.

An e-recorded deed must come through Simplifile, and mostly from professionals. The Recorder runs no e-recording platform of its own. Private companies, including CSC Global, ePN, Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile, send documents in for recording and may add their own charges.

A deed that transfers real property can be e-recorded through the Auditor, Engineer and Recorder, but only via Simplifile, and it has to come from a title company, bank or similar entity. Individuals may e-record other documents through Simplifile, but an individual's e-recording cannot transfer property. If e-recording is out of reach, mail the deed or bring it to the 18th floor.

The Recorder also accepts documents completed with electronic and online notarization that meet Ohio legislature and Secretary of State requirements.

Enclose a self-addressed, stamped envelope and the original deed comes back by mail. Without one, the Recorder charges postage or the $1 return fee.

Regular filers can open an escrow account at the Recorder with a starting deposit of $100 or more, so they do not bring a check for each filing. Certain public servants whose home addresses are exempt from public record may ask to have the address redacted from documents posted on the Recorder's website. They use the Request to Redact Address form and email it to the Recorder.

sections.h2: What to bring to the courthouse
sections.html:
Gather these items so one trip covers the Auditor and the Recorder:

  • The signed, notarized deed with a legal description copied from the prior recorded deed
  • The Auditor's payment: cash, business check or cashier's check for the transfer and conveyance charges
  • A second payment made out to the Franklin County Recorder, so the Auditor can forward the deed
  • A self-addressed, stamped envelope for the original
  • Proof of homestead status if the seller receives the exemption, since it lowers the conveyance fee

The Recorder's fee calculator and the Auditor's transfer calculator both help you total these amounts before you leave home. Add the two payments together on paper, then double check that each check names the right office, because a check made out to the wrong payee is refused and costs you the trip.

In a cash sale the title company or attorney usually assembles this packet for you. Your part is to sign in front of the notary and tell them whether you receive the homestead exemption. Ask whether they plan to use Simplifile, since e-recording of a property transfer is limited to a title company, bank or similar entity and an individual cannot do it alone.

Columbus is the county seat and the state capital, and Franklin County had 1,323,807 residents in 2020, the most of any Ohio county. Suburbs such as Bexley, Dublin, Gahanna, Grandview Heights, Grove City, Hilliard, New Albany, Upper Arlington, Westerville and Worthington all record deeds at this same courthouse. A house in Dublin and a house in Whitehall follow the same path through the Auditor and then the Recorder, so a complete packet saves a second trip.

faqs.q: How much does the Franklin County Recorder charge for a deed?
faqs.a: The Recorder lists $34 for the first two pages and $8 for each additional page. A $20 fee applies if the document misses the standardization requirements, and cards carry a 3% convenience fee.

faqs.q: Do I file with the Auditor or the Recorder first in Franklin County?
faqs.a: The Auditor first. After the transfer is complete, the deed goes to the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards it if you included a separate payment for the Recorder.

faqs.q: Does a deed need a notary in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes. All transfers must be signed in front of a notary, and electronic or online notarization is accepted when it meets Ohio requirements.

faqs.q: What is the Franklin County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: It is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, with a $3 minimum and a $0.50 transfer tax. The fee drops to $1 per $1,000 if the seller receives the homestead exemption.

faqs.q: Can an individual e-record a deed in Franklin County?
faqs.a: An individual can use Simplifile for some documents, but an individual's e-recording cannot transfer property. Deeds that transfer property come through a title company, bank or similar entity.
